title: Hihaze: One-Step Diffusion forHigh-Resolution Real-World Image Dehazing

paper.title: Hihaze: One-Step Diffusion for High-Resolution Real-World Image Dehazing
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models have recently achieved encouraging results in real-world image dehazing. However, restoring high-resolution images remains challenging due to spatially non-uniform haze and inconsistent predictions across local patches. To address these issues, we propose Hihaze, a one-step diffusion framework for high-resolution real-world dehazing. Hihaze adopts two haze-aware modulation modules: attentive skip compensation (ASC) and a spatial degradation adapter (SDA). ASC selectively transfers reliable encoder information to the variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder, preserving structural details while suppressing haze-degraded features. SDA extracts multi-scale spatial degradation representations and injects them into the U-Net to guide restoration according to local haze variations. Furthermore, we design a training-free global-guided patch fusion (GPF) method. It uses a global prediction to align patch appearance and downweight unreliable predictions, followed by structure-guided detail compensation. Notably, this training-free design also makes GPF a plug-and-play module for other dehazing models. Experiments across four real-world benchmarks show that Hihaze surpasses state-of-the-art approaches in both visual quality and inference speed. Specifically, it delivers PSNR improvements of 3.62 dB on Dense-Haze and 3.69 dB on NH-HAZE compared with the strongest baselines. Code: https://github.com/zhengchen1999/Hihaze .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Single-image dehazing reconstructs haze-free scenes from hazy inputs. Haze reduces contrast, shifts colors, and obscures details with spatially varying density. Physically, this degradation is formulated via the atmospheric scattering model ( Narasimhan & Nayar, 2002 ; McCartney & Hall Jr, 1977 ) 𝐈 ⁡ ( x ) = 𝐈 c ​ ( x ) ​ t h ​ ( x ) + 𝐀 ⁡ ( 1 − t h ​ ( x ) ) , \mathbf{I}(x)=\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{c}}(x)\,t_{\mathrm{h}}(x)+\mathbf{A}\bigl(1-t_{\mathrm{h}}(x)\bigr), (1) where 𝐈 \mathbf{I} and 𝐈 c \mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{c}} denote the hazy image and its clean counterpart. 𝐀 \mathbf{A} is the atmospheric light, and t h ​ ( x ) t_{\mathrm{h}}(x) is the transmission at pixel x x . Recovering 𝐈 c \mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{c}} is ill-posed because the scattering parameters are unknown. Early methods use statistical priors, such as dark-channel sparsity ( He et al., 2010 ) , to constrain restoration. However, these assumptions may fail in complex scenes. Later CNN- and Transformer-based methods learn restoration mappings from data ( Cai et al., 2016 ; Liu et al., 2019 ; Qin et al., 2020 ; Guo et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2022 ) . Despite this progress, recovering realistic textures remains difficult under dense, spatially varying haze. Recently, large pretrained diffusion models have provided rich generative priors for image restoration ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . They help recover realistic textures from degraded inputs. For dehazing, existing approaches exploit these priors through realistic haze synthesis, unpaired training, and physical or textual guidance ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Lan et al., 2025a ) . To reduce computation, latent diffusion performs denoising in a compact latent space ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . Further reducing the number of denoising steps accelerates inference and makes diffusion-based dehazing more practical ( Song et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . Nevertheless, two difficulties remain in high-resolution real-world dehazing: (1) Spatially non-uniform haze. VAE compression can discard fine details. Encoder–decoder skip connections help retain input information ( Lan et al., 2025a ) . However, encoder features contain both scene structures and haze degradation. Directly transferring them may leave residual haze in the result. Moreover, high-level semantic guidance does not explicitly describe local degradation. It therefore provides limited guidance for spatially varying restoration. Effective dehazing requires reliable detail transmission together with spatial degradation guidance. (2) Inconsistent patch predictions. High-resolution inference often uses patches to limit memory use ( Wang et al., 2024a ) . Each patch sees only part of the scene. Adjacent patches may therefore differ in color, illumination, and dehazing strength. Overlapping inference and local aggregation can reduce boundary artifacts ( Özdenizci & Legenstein, 2023 ; Ding et al., 2024 ) . However, they lack an explicit global reference. Averaging inconsistent predictions may also blur fine textures. Figure 1: Visual results on NH-HAZE 51 (left), I-HAZE 34 (upper right), and O-HAZE 01 (lower right). Each scene shows the hazy input on the left of the diagonal and the Hihaze result on the right. Bottom: matched details from the marked region of NH-HAZE 51. Hihaze removes haze while recovering scene structures and textures in the restored images. To address these issues, we propose Hihaze for high-resolution image dehazing. Hihaze adapts a pretrained latent diffusion model to restore hazy images in one step. We introduce two haze-aware modulation modules: attentive skip compensation (ASC) and a spatial degradation adapter (SDA). (1) ASC uses decoder features to retrieve reliable encoder information. It compensates for missing structures and fine details while suppressing haze-degraded features. (2) SDA extracts spatial degradation features from the hazy input. It injects these features into the U-Net at multiple scales. This guides restoration according to local haze variations. Moreover, we design training-free global-guided patch fusion (GPF) for high-resolution inference. A prediction from the downsampled full image provides a shared appearance reference. GPF aligns local patch predictions with this reference and reduces the contribution of inconsistent patches. Structural agreement between the fused result and the hazy input then guides detail compensation. This improves cross-patch consistency while preserving reliable textures. GPF can also be integrated into other dehazing models as a plug-and-play module. Extensive experiments on four real-world benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Hihaze. As shown in Fig. 1 , Hihaze removes more haze than the compared methods. It also recovers clearer edges and textures, even in severely degraded regions. Our main contributions are as follows: • We propose Hihaze, a one-step diffusion dehazing framework with attentive skip compensation and a spatial degradation adapter for high-resolution images. • We introduce global-guided patch fusion to improve consistency and preserve fine textures. It is a training-free, plug-and-play module for other dehazing models. • We validate Hihaze on four real-world benchmarks. It achieves superior reconstruction fidelity and perceptual quality under diverse haze conditions.

sections.heading: 2.1 Image Dehazing
sections.text: Early dehazing methods typically derive physical priors from natural-image statistics. Such constraints are subsequently coupled with the physical scattering formulation to restore haze-free images ( Fattal, 2008 ; He et al., 2010 ; Meng et al., 2013 ; Fattal, 2014 ; Berman et al., 2016 ) . Specifically, He et al. (2010) developed the Dark Channel Prior (DCP), noting that the minimum intensity across RGB channels within a haze-free local patch typically approaches zero. Similarly, Fattal (2014) proposed the Color-Line Prior, leveraging the one-dimensional distributions formed by pixels in local image patches in RGB color space to estimate scene transmission. However, handcrafted priors often struggle to model complex haze in real-world scenes, potentially causing color distortions. Driven by advances in deep learning, single-image dehazing increasingly relies on deep neural networks. With task-specific architectures, these models directly map hazy inputs to haze-free outputs ( Liu et al., 2019 ; Dong et al., 2020 ; Guo et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2022 ) . Although effective on synthetic benchmarks, these methods often generalize poorly to real-world scenes, where haze distributions are considerably more complex and diverse. To improve real-world generalization, recent works incorporate external priors or adaptive refinement mechanisms into the restoration pipeline ( Wu et al., 2023b ; Fang et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2025 ) . For example, RIDCP ( Wu et al., 2023b ) leverages high-quality codebook priors to guide the restoration of real-world hazy images. More recently, IPC-Dehaze ( Fu et al., 2025 ) employs an iterative predictor-critic framework that retains reliable codes and progressively refines code predictions. Nevertheless, constrained by limited generative capacity, standard CNN and Transformer architectures struggle to recover realistic details under heavy, spatially varying haze.

sections.heading: 2.2 Diffusion Model-Based Image Restoration
sections.text: Recent breakthroughs in diffusion models have shown remarkable capacity for complex image generation ( Song et al., 2020 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Ruiz et al., 2023 ) . By capturing rich priors of natural scenes, these generative frameworks have been widely adopted across various restoration tasks with compelling results ( Saharia et al., 2022b ; Saharia et al., 2022a ; Lugmayr et al., 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . In the context of real-world image dehazing, DiffDehaze ( Wang et al., 2025 ) combines realistic haze synthesis with accelerated fidelity-preserving sampling to achieve efficient and faithful restoration. Diff-Dehazer ( Lan et al., 2025a ) combines unpaired bidirectional diffusion mapping with physical priors to improve real-world generalization. Despite these advances, existing methods remain limited in handling spatially non-uniform haze in real-world scenes, often resulting in uneven restoration across image regions and residual haze. Moreover, the high memory cost of diffusion models often necessitates patch-wise inference for high-resolution images, resulting in inconsistent predictions across patches and visible boundary artifacts ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Lan et al., 2025a ) . Existing approaches mitigate boundary artifacts through overlapping patch inference and local aggregation ( Özdenizci & Legenstein, 2023 ; Ding et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024a ) . Specifically, Patch-DM ( Ding et al., 2024 ) suppresses seam artifacts by assembling features across adjacent regions for shifted-patch prediction. However, such aggregation mainly enforces consistency between neighboring patches. Averaging predictions in overlapping regions may also attenuate fine high-frequency textures in the restored images. In this paper, we introduce a one-step diffusion framework for high-resolution real-world image dehazing that enables memory-efficient patch-wise inference and effectively handles non-uniform haze.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Figure 2: Overview of Hihaze. SDA guides spatially adaptive denoising, while ASC transfers reliable encoder features to the VAE decoder. GPF combines global and local predictions for high-resolution restoration with consistent appearance and preserved fine details. This section details Hihaze, our one-step diffusion approach designed to restore high-resolution hazy scenes. We first introduce the overall framework in Sec. 3.1 . We then describe attentive skip compensation (ASC) in Sec. 3.2 and the spatial degradation adapter (SDA) in Sec. 3.3 . ASC retrieves reliable encoder features for VAE decoding, while SDA guides denoising according to local haze variations. Finally, Sec. 3.4 presents training-free global-guided patch fusion (GPF) for appearance consistency and structure-guided detail compensation. Training details are provided in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 3.2 Attentive Skip Compensation
sections.text: Latent diffusion models reduce computational cost through VAE compression, but this may attenuate fine spatial details. Encoder–decoder skip connections help recover these details by reusing input features ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Lan et al., 2025a ; Ai et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2022 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . However, spatially non-uniform haze causes the reliability of encoder features to vary across regions. Some regions retain useful scene details, whereas others are more severely affected by haze. Direct feature transfer can therefore introduce degraded information along with useful details. To address this variation, we propose attentive skip compensation (ASC). It selectively retrieves reliable encoder information and adaptively refines less reliable features during reconstruction. At stage ℓ \ell , ASC takes encoder and decoder features 𝐄 ℓ \mathbf{E}_{\ell} and 𝐃 ℓ \mathbf{D}_{\ell} . Decoder features then query encoder features through local cross-attention, with reliability guiding the selection of source information. This design retains reliable encoder information and focuses refinement on less reliable regions. It supports detail reconstruction while reducing the influence of haze-degraded features.

sections.heading: 3.3 Spatial Degradation Adapter
sections.text: Spatially non-uniform haze attenuates contrast and structural information to varying degrees across an image, leading to different restoration needs. To effectively handle spatially varying haze degradation, we introduce the spatial degradation adapter (SDA). It extracts multi-scale haze-aware features from the hazy input and injects them into the U-Net to guide spatially adaptive restoration. Haze representation. Given a hazy image 𝐈 \mathbf{I} , we use a convolutional encoder to learn multi-scale haze representations { 𝐅 ℓ } ℓ = 1 3 \{\mathbf{F}_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{3} that capture local degradation and restoration needs. The supervision targets and training details are provided in Appendix A.2.1 . To illustrate the haze information captured by SDA, we visualize the first channel of its finest-scale features in Fig. 3 . On NH-HAZE 55, the visible haze across the central region exhibits stronger responses, whereas the clearer upper-left region generally shows weaker responses. This spatial correspondence suggests that the learned features are sensitive to variations in haze distribution. Additional SDA feature visualizations on NH-HAZE and O-HAZE are provided in Appendix D.2 . Figure 3: Visualization of the first SDA feature channel on NH-HAZE 55 (left) and 14 (right). Both examples use the same color scale; warmer colors indicate stronger feature responses. U-Net adaptation. We align the haze features with three U-Net decoder stages, where convolutional adapters produce spatially gated residual corrections. At each scale, we inject features as: 𝐅 d ′ = 𝐅 d + Adapter ⁡ ( 𝐅 d , 𝐅 ) , \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{d}}^{\prime}=\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{d}}+\operatorname{Adapter}(\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{d}},\mathbf{F}), (6) where 𝐅 \mathbf{F} denotes haze features, 𝐅 d \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{d}} and 𝐅 d ′ \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{d}}^{\prime} are decoder features before and after injection, respectively, and Adapter \operatorname{Adapter} denotes the convolutional adapter. We also use the haze features to modulate the U-Net noise prediction, yielding ϵ ′ \bm{\epsilon}^{\prime} . Both feature and noise correction branches use zero-initialized output projections to preserve the original network output at initialization. Through multi-scale feature injection and noise prediction refinement, SDA incorporates spatially varying haze information into one-step denoising, adapting restoration to local degradation.

sections.heading: 3.4 Global-Guided Patch Fusion
sections.text: Figure 4: Overview of global-guided patch fusion (GPF). A global prediction guides patch alignment and reliability-aware fusion. Structural cues from the hazy input guide detail compensation. High-resolution diffusion-based dehazing often relies on patch-wise inference to accommodate limited GPU memory. However, each patch observes only partial scene context, which can lead to inconsistent color and illumination across regions. Averaging overlapping predictions can alleviate boundary artifacts, but cannot ensure global appearance consistency and may smooth fine details. To overcome these issues, we introduce global-guided patch fusion (GPF), a training-free strategy that combines global appearance guidance with local detail preservation. As illustrated in Fig. 4 , a prediction from the downsampled full image provides a common appearance reference, while original-resolution patch predictions supply complementary fine details. GPF consists of three components: appearance alignment, reliability-aware fusion, and detail compensation. Appearance alignment. For each local prediction 𝐏 i \mathbf{P}_{i} , we combine its multiscale wavelet high-frequency component with the low-frequency component of the corresponding global region 𝐆 i \mathbf{G}_{i} . This preserves local structures while establishing a consistent global appearance. Reliability-aware fusion. Appearance alignment preserves local details by retaining the high-frequency component of each patch prediction. However, patch predictions may contain artifacts due to limited scene context. We therefore assess the reliability of each raw patch prediction against the global reference and use it to control the contribution of the aligned prediction during fusion. We downsample each raw patch prediction to the native resolution of the global branch. We then compute its PSNR-Y against the corresponding global region. A sigmoid mapping converts this score into a reliability weight q i q_{i} . Consistent patches receive higher weights to preserve local details. Inconsistent patches contribute less and rely more on the global reference. To avoid abrupt transitions between patches, we aggregate their reliability weights using cosine windows 𝐰 i \mathbf{w}_{i} and apply Gaussian smoothing 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . The resulting spatial reliability map 𝐪 ¯ \bar{\mathbf{q}} controls the blending of aligned local predictions with the global reference: 𝐪 ¯ = 𝒮 ⁡ ( ∑ i 𝐰 i ​ q i ∑ i 𝐰 i ) , 𝐏 ^ i = 𝐪 ¯ i ⊙ [ 𝒲 H ​ ( 𝐏 i ) + 𝒲 L ​ ( 𝐆 i ) ] + ( 1 − 𝐪 ¯ i ) ⊙ 𝐆 i . \bar{\mathbf{q}}=\mathcal{S}\!\left(\frac{\sum_{i}\mathbf{w}_{i}q_{i}}{\sum_{i}\mathbf{w}_{i}}\right),\quad\widehat{\mathbf{P}}_{i}=\bar{\mathbf{q}}_{i}\odot\left[\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathbf{P}_{i})+\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{L}}(\mathbf{G}_{i})\right]+(1-\bar{\mathbf{q}}_{i})\odot\mathbf{G}_{i}. (7) 𝐆 i \mathbf{G}_{i} and 𝐪 ¯ i \bar{\mathbf{q}}_{i} denote the corresponding crops of the global prediction and reliability map, respectively. The operators 𝒲 H \mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{H}} and 𝒲 L \mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{L}} extract the wavelet high- and low-frequency components, respectively. Combining the two wavelet components yields the prediction produced by appearance alignment. Reliable regions retain more local information, while unreliable regions rely more on the global prediction. Finally, we aggregate the corrected patches using reliability weights and cosine windows: 𝐈 f = ∑ i q i ​ 𝐰 i ⊙ 𝐏 ^ i ∑ i q i ​ 𝐰 i . \mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{f}}=\frac{\sum_{i}q_{i}\mathbf{w}_{i}\odot\widehat{\mathbf{P}}_{i}}{\sum_{i}q_{i}\mathbf{w}_{i}}. We therefore use structural information retained in the hazy input to compensate for detail loss in the fused result. First, we estimate a local structural agreement map 𝐬 \mathbf{s} between the hazy input 𝐈 \mathbf{I} and the fused result 𝐈 f \mathbf{I}^{\mathrm{f}} . Its values lie in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] and guide spatially adaptive detail compensation. Regions with stronger structural agreement retain more restored details and receive more detail from the input. Regions with weaker agreement have attenuated detail responses, reducing the influence of inconsistent structures. Finally, we combine compensated details with low-frequency information from the fused result to reconstruct the output 𝐈 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{I}} . sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Settings
sections.text: Datasets. Model training uses paired hazy and clean images from LMHaze ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) and RW2AH ( Fang et al., 2025 ) . For evaluation, we adopt four real-world benchmarks covering diverse degradation conditions: indoor scenes in I-HAZE ( Ancuti et al., 2018b ) , outdoor environments in O-HAZE ( Ancuti et al., 2018a ) , heavy homogeneous haze in Dense-Haze ( Ancuti et al., 2019 ) , and spatially varying haze in NH-HAZE ( Ancuti et al., 2020 ) . We evaluate our model and other methods on all four datasets without fine-tuning on the target datasets. Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate reconstruction fidelity with PSNR and SSIM ( Wang et al., 2004 ) , and perceptual agreement with LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) and DISTS ( Ding et al., 2020 ) . FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) measures distributional differences in feature space between restored images and clean references. Q-Align ( Wu et al., 2023a ) provides no-reference quality scores. Implementation Details. We initialize the network from Stable Diffusion 2.1-base ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) and use LoRA with rank 16. With AdamW ( Loshchilov et al., 2017 ) , we train the U-Net LoRA and ASC for 200,000 iterations on 512 512 × \times 512 512 crops. We then train the SDA encoder on 512 512 × \times 512 512 crops and the U-Net adaptation branches on 1,024 × 1,024 1{,}024\times 1{,}024 crops for 10,000 iterations each. Inference uses one denoising step at t t = = 399 399 ; high-resolution images are processed with overlapping 1,024 × 1,024 1{,}024\times 1{,}024 patches and GPF. Appendix A in the supplementary material documents the training procedure, losses, learning rates, batch sizes, and other settings.

sections.heading: 4.2 Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods
sections.text: Compared Methods. We compare our method with eight representative dehazing approaches. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We have presented Hihaze, a single-step latent diffusion approach tailored for restoring high-resolution hazy scenes. To handle spatially non-uniform haze, Hihaze employs ASC to preserve reliable encoder features and SDA to inject spatial degradation information into one-step dehazing. Moreover, GPF uses a global prediction to guide local patch fusion, improving cross-patch consistency while preserving fine details. Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks demonstrate superior restoration quality and inference efficiency across diverse haze conditions.

sections.heading: Appendix A Training Strategy and Implementation Details
sections.text: We train Hihaze in two stages. In Stage 1, we jointly train the restoration backbone and ASC. In Stage 2, we freeze the base restoration model and sequentially train the SDA encoder and adaptation branches. GPF requires no training.

sections.heading: A.1 Backbone and ASC Training
sections.text: We initialize the model from Stable Diffusion 2.1-base and train the U-Net LoRA parameters, ASC and its feature-fusion layers, and a shared learnable text embedding. The remaining pretrained parameters are kept frozen. The LoRA rank and scaling parameter are both set to 16. The restoration loss is defined as ℒ b = ℒ 1 + λ pal ​ ℒ pal + λ per ​ ℒ per + λ adv ​ ℒ adv , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{b}}=\mathcal{L}_{1}+\lambda_{\mathrm{pal}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pal}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{per}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{per}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{adv}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adv}}, (10) where ℒ 1 \mathcal{L}_{1} is the L1 reconstruction loss, ℒ pal \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pal}} is the affinely aligned pixel loss (PAL) ( Li et al., 2026b ) , and ℒ per \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{per}} is the sum of DISTS losses on RGB images and their Scharr edge-magnitude maps ( Li et al., 2026a ) . We set λ pal = 0.8 \lambda_{\mathrm{pal}}=0.8 , λ per = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{per}}=1 , and λ adv = 0.1 \lambda_{\mathrm{adv}}=0.1 . PAL uses an affine RGB transformation with a bias term and a ridge regularization coefficient of 10 − 3 10^{-3} , with gradients stopped through the fitted transformation. The adversarial loss is computed using a DINOv3-based discriminator ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) . Its ConvNeXt-Large feature extractor is frozen, while its head is updated alternately with the restoration model. sections.heading: A.2.2 Adaptation Branch Training
sections.text: We then freeze the SDA encoder and train only the three adaptation branches in the U-Net decoder and the noise-correction branch. Their output projections are zero-initialized. Training uses the same restoration loss and weights as in Stage 1, with an additional mean squared penalty on the noise correction weighted by 10 − 5 10^{-5} . The entire discriminator remains frozen. The L1, PAL, and adversarial losses are computed on 1,024 × 1,024 1{,}024\times 1{,}024 crops, while the RGB and edge DISTS losses are evaluated after resizing the images to 512 × 512 512\times 512 .

Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Abstract Diffusion models have recently achieved encouraging results in real-world image dehazing. However, restoring high-resolution images remains challenging due to spatially non-uniform haze and inconsistent predictions across local patches. To address these issues, we propose Hihaze, a one-step diffusion framework for high-resolution real-world dehazing. Hihaze adopts two haze-aware modulation modules: attentive skip compensation (ASC) and a spatial degradation adapter (SDA). ASC selectively transfers reliable encoder information to the variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder, preserving structural details while suppressing haze-degraded features. SDA extracts multi-scale spatial degradation representations and injects them into the U-Net to guide restoration according to local haze variations. Furthermore, we design a training-free global-guided patch fusion (GPF) method. It uses a global prediction to align patch appearance and downweight unreliable predictions, followed by structure-guided detail compensation. Notably, this training-free design also makes GPF a plug-and-play module for other dehazing models. Experiments across four real-world benchmarks show that Hihaze surpasses state-of-the-art approaches in both visual quality and inference speed. Specifically, it delivers PSNR improvements of 3.62 dB on Dense-Haze and 3.69 dB on NH-HAZE compared with the strongest baselines. Code: https://github.com/zhengchen1999/Hihaze . 1 Introduction Single-image dehazing reconstructs haze-free scenes from hazy inputs. Haze reduces contrast, shifts colors, and obscures details with spatially varying density. Physically, this degradation is formulated via the atmospheric scattering model ( Narasimhan & Nayar, 2002 ; McCartney & Hall Jr, 1977 ) 𝐈 ⁡ ( x ) = 𝐈 c ​ ( x ) ​ t h ​ ( x ) + 𝐀 ⁡ ( 1 − t h ​ ( x ) ) , \mathbf{I}(x)=\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{c}}(x)\,t_{\mathrm{h}}(x)+\mathbf{A}\bigl(1-t_{\mathrm{h}}(x)\bigr), (1) where 𝐈 \mathbf{I} and 𝐈 c \mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{c}} denote the hazy image and its clean counterpart. 𝐀 \mathbf{A} is the atmospheric light, and t h ​ ( x ) t_{\mathrm{h}}(x) is the transmission at pixel x x . Recovering 𝐈 c \mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{c}} is ill-posed because the scattering parameters are unknown. Early methods use statistical priors, such as dark-channel sparsity ( He et al., 2010 ) , to constrain restoration. However, these assumptions may fail in complex scenes. Later CNN- and Transformer-based methods learn restoration mappings from data ( Cai et al., 2016 ; Liu et al., 2019 ; Qin et al., 2020 ; Guo et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2022 ) . Despite this progress, recovering realistic textures remains difficult under dense, spatially varying haze. Recently, large pretrained diffusion models have provided rich generative priors for image restoration ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . They help recover realistic textures from degraded inputs. For dehazing, existing approaches exploit these priors through realistic haze synthesis, unpaired training, and physical or textual guidance ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Lan et al., 2025a ) . To reduce computation, latent diffusion performs denoising in a compact latent space ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . Further reducing the number of denoising steps accelerates inference and makes diffusion-based dehazing more practical ( Song et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . Nevertheless, two difficulties remain in high-resolution real-world dehazing: (1) Spatially non-uniform haze. VAE compression can discard fine details. Encoder–decoder skip connections help retain input information ( Lan et al., 2025a ) . However, encoder features contain both scene structures and haze degradation. Directly transferring them may leave residual haze in the result. Moreover, high-level semantic guidance does not explicitly describe local degradation. It therefore provides limited guidance for spatially varying restoration. Effective dehazing requires reliable detail transmission together with spatial degradation guidance. (2) Inconsistent patch predictions. High-resolution inference often uses patches to limit memory use ( Wang et al., 2024a ) . Each patch sees only part of the scene. Adjacent patches may therefore differ in color, illumination, and dehazing strength. Overlapping inference and local aggregation can reduce boundary artifacts ( Özdenizci & Legenstein, 2023 ; Ding et al., 2024 ) . However, they lack an explicit global reference. Averaging inconsistent predictions may also blur fine textures. Figure 1: Visual results on NH-HAZE 51 (left), I-HAZE 34 (upper right), and O-HAZE 01 (lower right). Each scene shows the hazy input on the left of the diagonal and the Hihaze result on the right. Bottom: matched details from the marked region of NH-HAZE 51. Hihaze removes haze while recovering scene structures and textures in the restored images. To address these issues, we propose Hihaze for high-resolution image dehazing. Hihaze adapts a pretrained latent diffusion model to restore hazy images in one step. We introduce two haze-aware modulation modules: attentive skip compensation (ASC) and a spatial degradation adapter (SDA). (1) ASC uses decoder features to retrieve reliable encoder information. It compensates for missing structures and fine details while suppressing haze-degraded features. (2) SDA extracts spatial degradation features from the hazy input. It injects these features into the U-Net at multiple scales. This guides restoration according to local haze variations. Moreover, we design training-free global-guided patch fusion (GPF) for high-resolution inference. A prediction from the downsampled full image provides a shared appearance reference. GPF aligns local patch predictions with this reference and reduces the contribution of inconsistent patches. Structural agreement between the fused result and the hazy input then guides detail compensation. This improves cross-patch consistency while preserving reliable textures. GPF can also be integrated into other dehazing models as a plug-and-play module. Extensive experiments on four real-world benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Hihaze. As shown in Fig. 1 , Hihaze removes more haze than the compared methods. It also recovers clearer edges and textures, even in severely degraded regions. Our main contributions are as follows: • We propose Hihaze, a one-step diffusion dehazing framework with attentive skip compensation and a spatial degradation adapter for high-resolution images. • We introduce global-guided patch fusion to improve consistency and preserve fine textures. It is a training-free, plug-and-play module for other dehazing models. • We validate Hihaze on four real-world benchmarks. It achieves superior reconstruction fidelity and perceptual quality under diverse haze conditions. 2 Related Work 2.1 Image Dehazing Early dehazing methods typically derive physical priors from natural-image statistics. Such constraints are subsequently coupled with the physical scattering formulation to restore haze-free images ( Fattal, 2008 ; He et al., 2010 ; Meng et al., 2013 ; Fattal, 2014 ; Berman et al., 2016 ) . Specifically, He et al. (2010) developed the Dark Channel Prior (DCP), noting that the minimum intensity across RGB channels within a haze-free local patch typically approaches zero. Similarly, Fattal (2014) proposed the Color-Line Prior, leveraging the one-dimensional distributions formed by pixels in local image patches in RGB color space to estimate scene transmission. However, handcrafted priors often struggle to model complex haze in real-world scenes, potentially causing color distortions. Driven by advances in deep learning, single-image dehazing increasingly relies on deep neural networks. With task-specific architectures, these models directly map hazy inputs to haze-free outputs ( Liu et al., 2019 ; Dong et al., 2020 ; Guo et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2022 ) . Although effective on synthetic benchmarks, these methods often generalize poorly to real-world scenes, where haze distributions are considerably more complex and diverse. To improve real-world generalization, recent works incorporate external priors or adaptive refinement mechanisms into the restoration pipeline ( Wu et al., 2023b ; Fang et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2025 ) . For example, RIDCP ( Wu et al., 2023b ) leverages high-quality codebook priors to guide the restoration of real-world hazy images. More recently, IPC-Dehaze ( Fu et al., 2025 ) employs an iterative predictor-critic framework that retains reliable codes and progressively refines code predictions. Nevertheless, constrained by limited generative capacity, standard CNN and Transformer architectures struggle to recover realistic details under heavy, spatially varying haze. 2.2 Diffusion Model-Based Image Restoration Recent breakthroughs in diffusion models have shown remarkable capacity for complex image generation ( Song et al., 2020 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Ruiz et al., 2023 ) . By capturing rich priors of natural scenes, these generative frameworks have been widely adopted across various restoration tasks with compelling results ( Saharia et al., 2022b ; Saharia et al., 2022a ; Lugmayr et al., 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . In the context of real-world image dehazing, DiffDehaze ( Wang et al., 2025 ) combines realistic haze synthesis with accelerated fidelity-preserving sampling to achieve efficient and faithful restoration. Diff-Dehazer ( Lan et al., 2025a ) combines unpaired bidirectional diffusion mapping with physical priors to improve real-world generalization. Despite these advances, existing methods remain limited in handling spatially non-uniform haze in real-world scenes, often resulting in uneven restoration across image regions and residual haze. Moreover, the high memory cost of diffusion models often necessitates patch-wise inference for high-resolution images, resulting in inconsistent predictions across patches and visible boundary artifacts ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Lan et al., 2025a ) . Existing approaches mitigate boundary artifacts through overlapping patch inference and local aggregation ( Özdenizci & Legenstein, 2023 ; Ding et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024a ) . Specifically, Patch-DM ( Ding et al., 2024 ) suppresses seam artifacts by assembling features across adjacent regions for shifted-patch prediction. However, such aggregation mainly enforces consistency between neighboring patches. Averaging predictions in overlapping regions may also attenuate fine high-frequency textures in the restored images. In this paper, we introduce a one-step diffusion framework for high-resolution real-world image dehazing that enables memory-efficient patch-wise inference and effectively handles non-uniform haze. 3 Method Figure 2: Overview of Hihaze. SDA guides spatially adaptive denoising, while ASC transfers reliable encoder features to the VAE decoder. GPF combines global and local predictions for high-resolution restoration with consistent appearance and preserved fine details. This section details Hihaze, our one-step diffusion approach designed to restore high-resolution hazy scenes. We first introduce the overall framework in Sec. 3.1 . We then describe attentive skip compensation (ASC) in Sec. 3.2 and the spatial degradation adapter (SDA) in Sec. 3.3 . ASC retrieves reliable encoder features for VAE decoding, while SDA guides denoising according to local haze variations. Finally, Sec. 3.4 presents training-free global-guided patch fusion (GPF) for appearance consistency and structure-guided detail compensation. Training details are provided in Appendix A . 3.1 Overall Framework As shown in Fig. 2 , our restoration pipeline is constructed upon the pretrained Stable Diffusion 2.1-base backbone. Given a hazy image 𝐈 \mathbf{I} , the VAE encoder ℰ \mathcal{E} produces a latent representation 𝐳 I \mathbf{z}_{I} and intermediate features for subsequent reconstruction. This supports detail reconstruction while reducing the influence of unreliable haze-degraded encoder features during image reconstruction. For high-resolution inputs, we apply the same network to a downsampled full image and overlapping patches at the original resolution. The resulting global reference 𝐆 \mathbf{G} guides the alignment and fusion of local predictions { 𝐏 i } \{\mathbf{P}_{i}\} . GPF further uses structural agreement with the hazy input to compensate fine details, producing the final result 𝐈 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{I}} . Together, these designs enable spatially adaptive dehazing while maintaining global appearance consistency and preserving local structural details. 3.2 Attentive Skip Compensation Latent diffusion models reduce computational cost through VAE compression, but this may attenuate fine spatial details. Encoder–decoder skip connections help recover these details by reusing input features ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Lan et al., 2025a ; Ai et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2022 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . However, spatially non-uniform haze causes the reliability of encoder features to vary across regions. Some regions retain useful scene details, whereas others are more severely affected by haze. Direct feature transfer can therefore introduce degraded information along with useful details. To address this variation, we propose attentive skip compensation (ASC). It selectively retrieves reliable encoder information and adaptively refines less reliable features during reconstruction. At stage ℓ \ell , ASC takes encoder and decoder features 𝐄 ℓ \mathbf{E}_{\ell} and 𝐃 ℓ \mathbf{D}_{\ell} . A lightweight convolutional predictor with a sigmoid output estimates a spatial reliability map 𝐑 ℓ \mathbf{R}_{\ell} from both 𝐄 ℓ \mathbf{E}_{\ell} and 𝐃 ℓ \mathbf{D}_{\ell} . Decoder features then query encoder features through local cross-attention, with reliability guiding the selection of source information. For each window and attention head, the retrieved feature is 𝐕 ′ ℓ = softmax ⁡ ( 𝐐 ℓ ​ 𝐊 ℓ 𝖳 d + 𝐁 ℓ + log ⁡ ( max ⁡ { 𝐑 ℓ 𝖳 , ε } ) ) ​ 𝐕 ℓ , \mathbf{V^{\prime}}_{\ell}=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}\mathbf{K}_{\ell}^{\mathsf{T}}}{\sqrt{d}}+\mathbf{B}_{\ell}+\log\!\left(\max\{\mathbf{R}_{\ell}^{\mathsf{T}},\varepsilon\}\right)\right)\mathbf{V}_{\ell}, (4) where 𝐐 ℓ \mathbf{Q}_{\ell} and ( 𝐊 ℓ , 𝐕 ℓ ) (\mathbf{K}_{\ell},\mathbf{V}_{\ell}) are projected from normalized decoder and encoder features, respectively. The factor 1 1 − - 𝐑 ℓ \mathbf{R}_{\ell} increases correction weights at less reliable locations. The refined encoder features are concatenated with 𝐃 ℓ \mathbf{D}_{\ell} and processed by residual convolutional blocks, whose output is added to 𝐃 ℓ \mathbf{D}_{\ell} . This design retains reliable encoder information and focuses refinement on less reliable regions. It supports detail reconstruction while reducing the influence of haze-degraded features. 3.3 Spatial Degradation Adapter Spatially non-uniform haze attenuates contrast and structural information to varying degrees across an image, leading to different restoration needs. To effectively handle spatially varying haze degradation, we introduce the spatial degradation adapter (SDA). It extracts multi-scale haze-aware features from the hazy input and injects them into the U-Net to guide spatially adaptive restoration. Haze representation. Given a hazy image 𝐈 \mathbf{I} , we use a convolutional encoder to learn multi-scale haze representations { 𝐅 ℓ } ℓ = 1 3 \{\mathbf{F}_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{3} that capture local degradation and restoration needs. The supervision targets and training details are provided in Appendix A.2.1 . To illustrate the haze information captured by SDA, we visualize the first channel of its finest-scale features in Fig. 3 . On NH-HAZE 55, the visible haze across the central region exhibits stronger responses, whereas the clearer upper-left region generally shows weaker responses. This spatial correspondence suggests that the learned features are sensitive to variations in haze distribution. Additional SDA feature visualizations on NH-HAZE and O-HAZE are provided in Appendix D.2 . Figure 3: Visualization of the first SDA feature channel on NH-HAZE 55 (left) and 14 (right). Both examples use the same color scale; warmer colors indicate stronger feature responses. U-Net adaptation. We align the haze features with three U-Net decoder stages, where convolutional adapters produce spatially gated residual corrections. At each scale, we inject features as: 𝐅 d ′ = 𝐅 d + Adapter ⁡ ( 𝐅 d , 𝐅 ) , \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{d}}^{\prime}=\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{d}}+\operatorname{Adapter}(\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{d}},\mathbf{F}), (6) where 𝐅 \mathbf{F} denotes haze features, 𝐅 d \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{d}} and 𝐅 d ′ \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{d}}^{\prime} are decoder features before and after injection, respectively, and Adapter \operatorname{Adapter} denotes the convolutional adapter. We also use the haze features to modulate the U-Net noise prediction, yielding ϵ ′ \bm{\epsilon}^{\prime} . Both feature and noise correction branches use zero-initialized output projections to preserve the original network output at initialization. Through multi-scale feature injection and noise prediction refinement, SDA incorporates spatially varying haze information into one-step denoising, adapting restoration to local degradation. 3.4 Global-Guided Patch Fusion Figure 4: Overview of global-guided patch fusion (GPF). A global prediction guides patch alignment and reliability-aware fusion. Structural cues from the hazy input guide detail compensation. High-resolution diffusion-based dehazing often relies on patch-wise inference to accommodate limited GPU memory. However, each patch observes only partial scene context, which can lead to inconsistent color and illumination across regions. Averaging overlapping predictions can alleviate boundary artifacts, but cannot ensure global appearance consistency and may smooth fine details. To overcome these issues, we introduce global-guided patch fusion (GPF), a training-free strategy that combines global appearance guidance with local detail preservation. As illustrated in Fig. 4 , a prediction from the downsampled full image provides a common appearance reference, while original-resolution patch predictions supply complementary fine details. GPF consists of three components: appearance alignment, reliability-aware fusion, and detail compensation. Appearance alignment. For each local prediction 𝐏 i \mathbf{P}_{i} , we combine its multiscale wavelet high-frequency component with the low-frequency component of the corresponding global region 𝐆 i \mathbf{G}_{i} . This preserves local structures while establishing a consistent global appearance. Reliability-aware fusion. Appearance alignment preserves local details by retaining the high-frequency component of each patch prediction. However, patch predictions may contain artifacts due to limited scene context. We therefore assess the reliability of each raw patch prediction against the global reference and use it to control the contribution of the aligned prediction during fusion. We downsample each raw patch prediction to the native resolution of the global branch. We then compute its PSNR-Y against the corresponding global region. A sigmoid mapping converts this score into a reliability weight q i q_{i} . Consistent patches receive higher weights to preserve local details. Inconsistent patches contribute less and rely more on the global reference. To avoid abrupt transitions between patches, we aggregate their reliability weights using cosine windows 𝐰 i \mathbf{w}_{i} and apply Gaussian smoothing 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . We therefore use structural information retained in the hazy input to compensate for detail loss in the fused result. Regions with stronger structural agreement retain more restored details and receive more detail from the input. Regions with weaker agreement have attenuated detail responses, reducing the influence of inconsistent structures. Finally, we combine compensated details with low-frequency information from the fused result to reconstruct the output 𝐈 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{I}} . Model training uses paired hazy and clean images from LMHaze ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) and RW2AH ( Fang et al., 2025 ) . For evaluation, we adopt four real-world benchmarks covering diverse degradation conditions: indoor scenes in I-HAZE ( Ancuti et al., 2018b ) , outdoor environments in O-HAZE ( Ancuti et al., 2018a ) , heavy homogeneous haze in Dense-Haze ( Ancuti et al., 2019 ) , and spatially varying haze in NH-HAZE ( Ancuti et al., 2020 ) . We evaluate our model and other methods on all four datasets without fine-tuning on the target datasets. Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate reconstruction fidelity with PSNR and SSIM ( Wang et al., 2004 ) , and perceptual agreement with LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) and DISTS ( Ding et al., 2020 ) . FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) measures distributional differences in feature space between restored images and clean references. Q-Align ( Wu et al., 2023a ) provides no-reference quality scores. Implementation Details. We initialize the network from Stable Diffusion 2.1-base ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) and use LoRA with rank 16. With AdamW ( Loshchilov et al., 2017 ) , we train the U-Net LoRA and ASC for 200,000 iterations on 512 512 × \times 512 512 crops. We then train the SDA encoder on 512 512 × \times 512 512 crops and the U-Net adaptation branches on 1,024 × 1,024 1{,}024\times 1{,}024 crops for 10,000 iterations each. Inference uses one denoising step at t t = = 399 399 ; high-resolution images are processed with overlapping 1,024 × 1,024 1{,}024\times 1{,}024 patches and GPF. Appendix A in the supplementary material documents the training procedure, losses, learning rates, batch sizes, and other settings. 4.2 Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods Compared Methods. We compare our method with eight representative dehazing approaches. The non-diffusion methods include PTTD ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , IPC-Dehaze ( Fu et al., 2025 ) , and BiLaLoRA ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . The diffusion-based methods include DiffUIR ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) , FCDM ( Wang et al., 2024b ) , Diff-Dehazer ( Lan et al., 2025a ) , DiffDehaze ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , and HazeFlow ( Shin et al., 2025 ) . Appendix C provides results for all six metrics on all four benchmarks, together with qualitative comparisons before and after applying GPF to further examine its effectiveness across different methods and haze conditions. 5 Conclusion We have presented Hihaze, a single-step latent diffusion approach tailored for restoring high-resolution hazy scenes. To handle spatially non-uniform haze, Hihaze employs ASC to preserve reliable encoder features and SDA to inject spatial degradation information into one-step dehazing. Moreover, GPF uses a global prediction to guide local patch fusion, improving cross-patch consistency while preserving fine details. Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks demonstrate superior restoration quality and inference efficiency across diverse haze conditions.
